The method$\,{\times}\,$task reversal is striking: attention-based scoring achieves 90--95\% on Long (rollout peaks at 94.8\%, seed43 confirms $\Delta{\leq}$0.6\,pp) versus L2's 45.0\%, but collapses to 0\% on Goal where L2 retains 61.0\%. On Object, all three variants achieve near-baseline performance (${\geq}$97.4\%), far exceeding both L2 (42.6\%) and random (70.6\%). On Spatial, rollout leads at 92.8\%. The mode ranking itself reverses across suites: last-layer attention is best on Object (99.2\%) but worst among attention methods on Spatial (88.8\%) and Long (90.2\%), while rollout shows the opposite pattern.

The reversal has a functional explanation. Long-horizon tasks involve sequential manipulation steps where the decoder's attention naturally focuses on task-relevant tokens at each step; attention scores capture this step-by-step relevance. Goal-conditioned tasks require reasoning about spatial relationships between the current state and a goal image; this demands precise spatial encoding that attention weights---which reflect decoder query patterns, not spatial information content---do not capture. L2 norms, as a proxy for activation magnitude, better preserve spatially informative tokens for goal-conditioned reasoning.
tool_args.new_text:
L2 norm selection is anti-informative on X-VLA's entangling connector: L2 falls below random on all four suites, with gaps ranging from $-$8.2\,pp (Goal) to $-$27.2\,pp (Object). Attention-based scoring recovers near-baseline performance across all suites (${\geq}$92.8\%), with rollout peaking at 94.8\% on Long (seed43 confirms $\Delta{\leq}$0.6\,pp). On Object, all three attention variants achieve ${\geq}$97.4\%, far exceeding both L2 (43.4\%) and random (70.6\%). The mode ranking reverses across suites: last-layer attention is best on Object (99.2\%) but worst among attention methods on Spatial (88.8\%) and Long (90.2\%), while rollout shows the opposite pattern.

The L2 failure has a structural explanation. The BART encoder's 12-layer self-attention redistributes information across tokens, equalizing activation magnitudes (CV$\,{=}\,$0.151). L2 norms no longer reflect token importance; instead, they select spatially correlated clusters that miss critical information. Goal L2 exhibits non-monotonic behavior ($k{=}0.7$: 53.4\% $<$ $k{=}0.5$: 59.0\%), confirming that retaining more L2-selected tokens is actively harmful. Per-task variance under L2 pruning is extreme on Spatial (std$\,{=}\,$31.5\,pp, range 0--92\%), while attention scoring keeps all tasks above 80\%. By contrast, $\pi_{0.5}$'s linear connector preserves per-token importance gradients, and L2 outperforms random by 17--34\,pp at high retention ($k{\geq}0.85$), confirming that scoring validity is architecture-dependent.
